lines.note: Ma is equated with mata, 'more' or 'again'. Ma hitotsu supplies the example 'one more'; the italic Ma- belongs instead to Portuguese Mais across the line break.

runs.text: is hum. ¶ Item, He particula que dà for-

lines.note: Is completes Mais hum, one more. The second explanation treats ma as a particle adding force or precision to the expression it accompanies.

runs.text: ça, & propriedade à palaura com que ſe ajun-

lines.note: Ça completes força. The particle joins another word and strengthens its sense; ajun- remains at the printed line edge rather than being expanded here.
Ta completes ajunta. Mamukae illustrates the intensifying prefix: directly opposite or fully facing something, matching muito de fronte.
Massugu ni means very straight or directly. The paragraph mark is visible and restored; re- begins rectamente below, while the two s-types remain as printed.
Ctamente completes rectamente. Ma-aonoki ni means fully turned onto one's back; the scan supports two adjacent a letters, agreeing with the repeated example below rather than OCR Mauonoqini.
Virado de costas completes the first explanation. The Japanese example combines ma-aonoki ni with an emphatic dôdo before the verb of falling on the next row.
Ochita completes the example: fell completely onto the back. The initial v is the historical romanization, and the Portuguese Cahio is not modernized.
Maba denotes eagle feathers used for arrows. The printed gloss gives their practical use without specifying a modern feather type or bird species more narrowly.
Mabara and mabara ni describe a scattered or disordered arrangement. Adu. belongs to the italic grammatical apparatus; Latin l introduces the alternative form.
The gloss continues 'in a scattered manner'. Mabara ni zat- begins the example of an uncoordinated retreat, with zatto divided between the rows.
Zatto hiita completes the example of drawing back in a scattered group. Yax. is the printed citation label; its wording is retained without replacing it with another source abbreviation.
The retreat is additionally described as without order. This closes the example rather than defining the following cavalry term.

runs.text: O remeter a caualo ſem ordem,

lines.note: Mabaragake denotes charging on horseback without a coordinated formation. The gloss begins with remeter a cavalo and qualifies the charge on the next row.
The charge lacks both order and cohesion. Mabaragake wo suru supplies the corresponding verbal expression, with the object particle attached in print.
Mabara is illustrated adjectivally in mabarana ninju, a scattered body of people. The unmarked ninju is retained rather than receiving a conjectural long-vowel accent.
Palhada completes espalhada: people dispersed and without order. This finishes the adjective example above.

runs.text: O não poder olhar fito pera o ſol,

lines.note: Mabayui concerns being dazzled, here the inability to look steadily at the sun. Portuguese fito means fixedly in this sentence and is not the Japanese word hito.

runs.text: ou pera outra couſa muito lucida. Vt,

lines.note: The same inability applies to another very bright object. Hi no begins the Japanese example explaining the dazzle caused by sunlight.
Hi no hikari ni yotte mabayui means being dazzled by the sun's light. The Portuguese says the eyes are blinded; the source of the brightness follows below.
The eyes are dazzled by the brightness of the sun. The scan supports the single word claridade rather than the OCR's erroneous internal space clarida de.
Mabayuu is the contracted adverbial form of mabayui. The marked u is visible, and Adu. supplies the grammatical classification without an additional gloss.
Mabayusa is the nominal form for the dazzling quality or sensation. It is printed alone and should not acquire a fabricated Portuguese continuation.

runs.text: Tributo, ou foro que ſe paga por ca-

lines.note: Mabet denotes a levy or ground rent measured by an area unit. The bare final t is preserved; ca- begins cada on the next row.

runs.text: da dous Tatamis ẽ quadro de chão. ¶

lines.note: The levy is charged for each stated two-tatami measure of ground. Tatamis is embedded in Portuguese prose; Ma- begins the Japanese payment example rather than another unit.

runs.text: Dar, ou pagar este foro de tã-

lines.note: Mabet wo dasu means paying or delivering this levy. The Portuguese specifies the charge for so much ground, with tã- continuing below.
To completes the abbreviated tanto across the line break. The land-area explanation ends here and does not belong to the following blinking entry.
Mabiki here means blinking the eyes. The example begins Ma- and should not be confused with the agricultural verb spelled alike below.
Mabiki mo sezu tatakoo means fighting without even blinking. The printed historical verb form tatacǒ is retained rather than modernized to tatakau.

runs.text: jar com os olhos. i, ſem medo.

lines.note: The translation completes 'without blinking the eyes', explained as without fear. The final X. is an upright regional-usage label, including its punctuation.
This mabiki is thinning a dense planting by removing seedlings. The principal parts remain diplomatic; the gloss's object is completed on the next row.

runs.text: couſa ſemeada que eſtà muito basta pera ſe deſ-

lines.note: The planting is too dense, and the removed material is intended for setting elsewhere. Preserve basta as printed and the division des- before por below.
Despor continues across the line break, meaning transplanting or setting out elsewhere. Yasai wo mabiku illustrates thinning vegetables; q is supported by the verb and visible type.
The Portuguese translates the example as thinning vegetables by pulling some out. The historical spelling ortaliça lacks the modern initial h and is retained.
Mabiki daikon are young radishes pulled during thinning. The gloss specifies their youth and removal, with the reason and use on the next row.

runs.text: por eſtarem muito baſtos, pera Xiru, &c.

lines.note: The radishes are pulled because they are crowded, for use in shiru or similar preparations. Xiru is an entire Japanese term within the Portuguese explanation; the OCR's one-letter font split is removed.
Mabikina and tsumamina name thinned greens or young turnips. The printed l, introduces an alternative, and ti- starts tirão below.

runs.text: rão do lugar onde eſtauão muito eſpeſſos, &

lines.note: The plants are removed from a place where they were growing too thickly. The scan supports eſpeſſos; OCR eſpelßos mistakes the long-s forms for an l and an unrelated letter.
Bastos completes the paired description of dense growth. This short physical continuation closes the thinning entry.
Maboraye means looking steadily or gazing. The OCR's leading long s is not a printed character, and olhos fitos has a visible word boundary.

The example describes an honored person gazing over a distant expanse of sea. The separate i before tamǒ is visible and belongs to the Japanese verbal construction; it should not disappear with the fallible kana hint.

runs.text: Lib. 4. Eſtaua vendo cõ os olhos

lines.note: Feiq. is the upright source label and Lib. 4 its italic book reference. The Portuguese begins 'was looking with the eyes', continuing the steady-gaze explanation below.

runs.text: fitos ſobre o mar largo, & estendido ao longe.

lines.note: The gaze is fixed over the broad sea stretching into the distance. The visible word is longe, not OCR lenge; no geographical identification is added.

Maborayete i nagara means remaining in the act of gazing. The lower-case i is separate in print. Second-pass enlargement resolves Aſsi as long ſ followed by short s and i, and confirms the small terminal hyphen in eſ-/taua across this and the next row.
Taua completes eſtaua across the line boundary, giving 'as he was with his eyes fixed'. This belongs to the preceding example and ends before the noun mabori.

runs.text: Nomina, ou relicario que ſe traz

lines.note: Mabori denotes an amulet or reliquary carried on the person. The scan supports traz, not OCR trac, and the location is specified on the following row.

The object is worn around the neck. Latin Aliquando introduces the occasional meaning 'guard' or 'protection'; visible i and capital G correct the OCR's Alquando and Cuarda. A comma follows Aliquando. The faint terminal punctuation after Guarda is retained as a comma, with nonblocking uncertainty, before ou proteição on the next column.
This completes the alternative protective sense of mabori. Preserve the historical spelling proteição rather than replacing it with a modern Portuguese form.
Mamori botoke denotes a protective Buddhist figure or image. The headword visibly has mamori, unlike neighboring mabori; Fotoque inside the Portuguese gloss is a separate embedded term.

runs.text: que ſe traz ao peſcoço por reliquia.

lines.note: The alternative is an image carried around the neck as a relic or protective object. This completes the preceding noun phrase rather than introducing another entry.
Mabori is guarding or defending. Preserve the historical b variant and its printed principal parts rather than replacing it with modern mamori.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Eſtar com os olhos fitos em algũa

lines.note: A second sense is keeping one's eyes fixed on something. This explains the connection between guarding and watching without conflating the two Portuguese glosses.
The example hito wo mabori tsumete iru concerns gazing continuously at someone. Iru remains an independent printed word, and the direct object is a person.

runs.text: Estar com os olhos fitos em alguem.

lines.note: The Portuguese confirms the fixed-gaze meaning of the preceding example. The provisional st allograph is retained rather than globally normalized.

runs.text: Maneira de ſonho leue que paſſa

lines.note: Maboroshi is described as a brief, light dream or vision. The verb passa continues into the adverbial qualification on the next row.

runs.text: breuemente em que ſe ve algũa couſa, ou figu-

lines.note: In this fleeting vision one sees some thing or figure. Figu- begins figura, and the source's unaccented ve is retained.

Ra completes figura, seen distinctly. The missing s in OCR ditinctamente is restored from the scan; the visibly comma-like final punctuation is retained rather than regularized to an entry-ending period.
Mabuka denotes something set deeply or pulled down low. Ami- starts amigasa, the woven hat in the example, not a Portuguese word.

Amigasa mabuka ni ficcôda describes pulling a woven hat low over the eyes. Second-pass enlargement confirms the doubled c, unlike OCR fiocôda. A circumflex is the chosen visible vowel mark, without inserting the nasalization expected from the Japanese form; this remains a nonblocking graphic caveat. Tac. is the citation label.
The Portuguese completes meteo o: he pulled the hat well down over the eyes. This supplies the practical sense of mabuca.
Mabuchi denotes the edges of the eyelids. Capellas is the dictionary's anatomical metaphor, matching the separate mabuta entry below.

runs.text: Eſtar ẽuolto ẽ algũa couſa co-

lines.note: Mabure concerns being covered or coated in a substance. Both nasal abbreviations and the visible co- division are preserved.

runs.text: mo ẽfarinhado, ou ẽlameado, &c. No Ximo

lines.note: Examples are being coated with flour or mud. Ximo is the Japanese regional designation inside Portuguese prose. Comparison with Ximo at c2-l026 supports italic lowercase letters here; the whole word is retained in the surrounding italic setting, rather than the OCR's isolated X font split.
The regional alternative is mameri. Doro ni mabu- starts the example of being covered in mud, continuing the main verb across the line break.
Ruru completes mabururu, translated as being muddy. The following figurative application is introduced by per met., not a Japanese source label.
Aku ni mabururu means being steeped or mired in evil. The Portuguese renders this figuratively as being infected and immersed, continuing below.

The gloss completes the image of being mired in wickedness. The displaced '(ſupra.' at the far right belongs logically with Vide on the next row, but is restored on this physical row with named right-hand segments.
The dictionary prefers mabori to this verbal variant maburi. Meliùs and Vide are italic apparatus; the displaced supra above completes 'see above' without being moved into this line.
The noun maburi likewise points to mabori. The printed target is upright after italic Vide., unlike the italicized target inside the preceding explanatory phrase.
Mabut pairs the terms ma and butsu, explained by tengu and hotoke. The Portuguese gloss uses Fotoque within its own wording; the roman Japanese synonyms are not typeface-toggle candidates.
Mabuta is the eyelid, described by capella do olho. This anatomical entry is distinct from both the religious compound before it and the coating verb after it.
Mabushi means mixing or coating something in another substance. Preserve the historical -uita principal part rather than replacing it with a modern -ushita form.

runs.text: mo Mochis em farinha de caſtanhas, ou couſa

lines.note: The example is coating mochi cakes in chestnut flour or something similar. Mochis is an embedded Japanese-derived term in the Portuguese sentence, not a new headword.
A regional Ximo alternative is mameshi, mamesu. The region name belongs to the Portuguese explanation, while the Japanese alternative begins after it.
Eita completes the alternative verb's principal parts. The dictionary calls it a good word; the next example begins doro ni mi wo ma-, coating one's body in mud.
Busu completes mabusu from the preceding row. The example means covering oneself with mud, translated by the reflexive enlamearse.
Makabura denotes the flesh or prominence of the brow. Ma- begins the repeated noun in the example on the following row.
Makabura no takai hito is a person with prominent brows. The final so belongs to sobrancelhas across the break and has no supplied hyphen.

runs.text: brancelhas altas, ou muito ſaidas pera fora.

lines.note: Brancelhas completes sobrancelhas. The brows are high or project outward; visible d supports ſaidas, not OCR ſaicas, without adding a modern accent.

runs.text: Sombra que faz a mão poſta ſobre os

lines.note: Makage is the shade produced by holding one's hand over the eyes. The hand is singular, and the gloss's object continues below.
Makage wo sasu illustrates making this shade with the hand. The Portuguese begins the action 'put the hand', continued on the next row.

runs.text: ſobre os olhos pera ver ao longe.

lines.note: The hand is placed above the eyes to see into the distance. This completes the practical explanation of the gesture.
Makai is described as an assembly or company of demons. The visible dia- replaces OCR diu- and continues as diabos below.
Bos completes diabos. Upright Bup. marks Buddhist terminology; its final period is not a separate italic run.
Makanai is managing or administering household affairs. Both principal-part vowels have carons; the Portuguese verb is divided adminis-trar.

runs.text: trar algũa couſa de caſa, renda, &c.

lines.note: Trar completes administrar. Household matters, income and similar concerns specify what is administered, rather than limiting makanai to food provision.
The noun makanai denotes household management or administration. It is a separate nominal entry following the verb's principal parts.
Makari is glossed with going, coming and being. The following explanation concerns its role with other verbs, beginning with the divided Quã-.

runs.text: do ſe ajunta a algũs verbos como ſe verà a bai

lines.note: Quando is completed, and the reader is directed to examples below. Preserve the unhyphenated bai at the edge; baixo continues on the next physical row.

runs.text: xo falos mais corteſes, & elegantes falando

lines.note: Xo completes baixo. The dictionary says attaching makari makes the verbs more courteous and elegant when speaking, with the relevant speaker completed below.
Hum de si completes the instruction: these courteous forms are used when speaking of oneself. The line is indented continuation text, not a flush-left headword.
Makarikaeri is returning, the first compound in the sequence illustrating makari. Preserve the historical cayeri spelling and its printed principal parts.
Makarikoomuri concerns receiving or hearing a message or command from a superior. The example below repeats the verb with an explicitly marked long o.
The message or command comes from a noble person. Xeixǒgun- begins the Japanese example's official designation; this indented row remains a continuation of the preceding entry.

runs.text: no xenjiuo macari cǒmutte taifeini xicai-

lines.note: The example receives the command and brings the world into peace. The scan clearly separates macari cǒmutte, uses a caron rather than OCR tilde, and reads xicai- rather than aucai-. Xicaiuo continues on f299; the isolated uo below is a catchword.
